title: Reduced effective resolution from averaging in attention
description: Self-attention reduces the number of operations to relate signals from distant positions to a constant, but at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions. Multi-Head Attention is used to counteract this effect.
canonical_description: attention aggregations reduce effective resolution due to averaging over positions

evidence.anchor: reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions
evidence.quote: In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section~[REF:sec:attention].

verdict.reasoning: Paper 1 (Laplacian Heads) is not_addressed — it focuses on controlling within-sequence variance and smoothing, which is orthogonal to the gap's concern about resolution loss from averaging. Paper 2 (Attention is Not All You Need) provides a partial_solution: it proves that pure self-attention converges doubly-exponentially to rank-1 (an extreme form of reduced effective resolution), and critically shows that multi-head attention does NOT counteract this — it accelerates rank collapse. This directly challenges the gap's claim that "Multi-Head Attention is used to counteract" reduced resolution. However, the gap remains partially open because: (1) the paper studies rank collapse (complete token uniformity) rather than "reduced effective resolution" as a general phenomenon, (2) it does not quantify effective resolution or propose architectural remedies specifically targeting averaging-induced resolution loss (it identifies skip connections and MLPs as mitigators for rank collapse, not for resolution loss per se). The gap's core problem — how averaging reduces resolution and what specifically counteracts it — is only partly addressed by disproving one proposed remedy.

paper.title: Laplacian Heads Improve Transformers by Smoothing Token Representations
paper.abstract: Transformers update token representations through multi-head attention and residual connections as $X \leftarrow X + \sum_{i} P^{(i)}XW_{V_i}W_{o_i}$, where $P^{(i)}$ is the softmax attention matrix in head $i$. We propose replacing a subset of $P^{(i)}$'s with the Laplacian $I - P^{(i)}$, giving $X \leftarrow X + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{A}} P^{(i)}XW_{V_i}W_{o_i} + \sum_{i \in \mathcal{L}} (I - P^{(i)})XW_{V_i}W_{o_i}$. Our proposal has two motivations. First, it allows attention heads to update the mean of token representations, while Laplacian heads can directly control within-sequence variance. Second, if tokens are viewed as nodes in a graph with edge weights $P^{(i)}$, then $I - P^{(i)}$ is the corresponding graph Laplacian, and the update can be interpreted as one step of heat diffusion on the graph. We show that this simple modification improves performance across supervised learning, language modeling, and self-supervised learning tasks. To investigate why, we examine the token representations learned with and without Laplacian heads. In supervised learning, Laplacian heads collapse token representations within the same sequence and align the sequence means with the geometry of Neural Collapse. In language modeling, they increase the separability of token representations that share the same next-token prediction. In self-supervised learning, they produce token representations whose principal components are better suited for segmentation. Across modalities, they also lead to faster-decaying spectra, indicating stronger token smoothing. Overall, our findings challenge the prevailing view that token oversmoothing is inherently harmful, showing instead that certain forms of smoothing can be beneficial.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes replacing a subset of standard attention heads with "Laplacian heads" that compute $(I-P^{(i)})XW_{V_i}W_{o_i}$ instead of $P^{(i)}XW_{V_i}W_{o_i}$. This gives the model direct control over within-sequence variance and performs graph diffusion on token representations. The paper shows this improves performance across image classification, language modeling, and self-supervised learning, and that Laplacian heads induce stronger token smoothing (faster spectral decay, increased within-sequence collapse).
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the problem of reduced effective resolution from averaging in attention. The gap concerns how attention's weighted averaging over positions loses fine-grained positional information, and how multi-head attention is used to counteract this. The Laplacian head modification is about controlling within-sequence variance and inducing smoothing/diffusion — a different concern entirely. The paper never mentions "effective resolution" or discusses resolution loss from averaging. In fact, Laplacian heads increase token smoothing (making tokens more similar), which would exacerbate rather than counteract resolution loss. The gap's specific problem — how averaging reduces resolution and how to mitigate it — remains entirely unaddressed.

paper.title: Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth
paper.abstract: Attention-based architectures have become ubiquitous in machine learning, yet our understanding of the reasons for their effectiveness remains limited. This work proposes a new way to understand self-attention networks: we show that their output can be decomposed into a sum of smaller terms, each involving the operation of a sequence of attention heads across layers. Using this decomposition, we prove that self-attention possesses a strong inductive bias towards "token uniformity". Specifically, without skip connections or multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), the output converges doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix. On the other hand, skip connections and MLPs stop the output from degeneration. Our experiments verify the identified convergence phenomena on different variants of standard transformer architectures.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper studies rank collapse in self-attention networks, proving that pure self-attention (without skip connections or MLPs) converges doubly-exponentially to a rank-1 matrix where all tokens become identical. This is a more extreme form of the "reduced effective resolution" problem described in the gap. The paper develops a path decomposition to analyze multi-head attention and shows that multi-head attention does NOT counteract rank collapse — in fact, more heads accelerate convergence to rank-1 (the bound includes H as a multiplicative factor). Instead, the paper identifies skip connections and MLPs as the mechanisms that counteract rank collapse.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific claim in the gap that "Multi-Head Attention is used to counteract" reduced effective resolution from averaging. In fact, the paper's results directly contradict this claim by showing that multi-head attention accelerates rank collapse (more heads = faster convergence to identical tokens). The gap concerns "reduced effective resolution" as a general phenomenon from averaging over positions, while the paper studies the more extreme case of complete rank collapse to identical tokens. The paper does not analyze or quantify "effective resolution" in the sense the gap describes — it focuses on rank (matrix rank) rather than resolution. Additionally, the paper's analysis is limited to the inductive bias toward token uniformity and does not propose architectural solutions specifically targeting the resolution loss from averaging in attention.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Moderately high feasibility. Key drivers: (1) The problem is analytical/theoretical — no data collection needed, only small-scale experiments on existing transformer architectures. (2) Compute requirements are modest: probing small transformers with synthetic data doesn't need frontier-scale resources. (3) Partial solutions exist (rank collapse theory) that provide a foundation, and the gap is well-scoped: formalize "effective resolution" (e.g., attention matrix rank, entropy, or effective number of attended positions), show how averaging degrades it, then test architectural remedies. (4) The main challenge is conceptual — defining what "effective resolution" means precisely — but there are multiple plausible formalizations. Evaluatability is reasonable: one can measure the proposed resolution metric in controlled settings and test whether modifications improve it while maintaining performance. Overall tractable for a small team with a theoretical bent.
